The prerequisite for theft

🔹A man took a fancy to becoming a thief, and to learn the trade professionally, he went to Nishapur, for he had heard that a skilled and seasoned thief lived there.

🔹When he entered the thief's house and stated his purpose, the master thief accepted him and took him on.

🔹Then, when they spread out the food cloth, the man reached out his right hand to eat, but the thief stopped him and said, "Eat with your left hand!" The man tried to eat with his left hand, but since he wasn't used to it, he couldn't, and he brought out his right hand again.

🔹The thief told him, "My son! On the path you've set out on, the very first step is that they cut off your right hand, because that is the religious law's ruling for a thief. Once they cut off your right hand, you must be able to eat with your left hand so you don't suffer."

🔹Hearing this, the man came to his senses and took heed. He said to himself, "For the sake of gaining a little silver and wire, it isn't wise to lose a hand this precious!" So right then and there, he put the whole idea of theft out of his mind and gave it up entirely.

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] The whisper of 12. The autumn season has arrived; an autumn that breathes with…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

The whisper of 12. The autumn season has arrived; an autumn that breathes with the blowing of its winds and the turning of its trees' leaves from green to yellow. The month of Mehr is bound to the name and memory of three luminous stars in the sky of Iranian culture and art; cherished souls whose long and deep companionship over the past three decades has polished my soul and gladdened my days: Hafez Shirazi, Sohrab Sepehri, and Mohammadreza Shajarian. Shajarian and Sepehri were born in the month of Mehr. The anniversary commemorating the thinking recluse of Shiraz also falls in this month. I am glad that the lecture series "In the Presence of Hafez" begins the day after tomorrow, in the month of Mehr. In this lecture series, I intend to offer my own re-reading and re-creation of thirty ghazals from the Divan of Hafez and to narrate my roughly forty years of familiarity and intimacy with Hafez's life-world here and now. The opening verse of the first ghazal I have chosen for re-reading and narrative-making is as follows: "If the Sufi drinks wine in measure, may it be sweet to him / Otherwise, may he forget the thought of this affair." Other exquisite verses are also found in this ghazal: "Our elder said no error befell the pen of creation / Bravo to his pure vision that covers errors!" and "The King of Turks listens to the words of claimants / May he be ashamed of the injustice done to the sweet Siyavash!" I have repeatedly read the verses of this stunning artistic work of Hafez over the past decades and have gazed upon them and into them. In this process and in the long future ahead, it is as though both I was reading the ghazal and the ghazal was reading me. For this reason, my present understanding of "pure vision that covers errors" and "shame from the injustice of Siyavash's blood" has noticeably changed. This epistemic transformation can also be explained in the language of Gadamerian hermeneutics and by borrowing the doctrine of the "fusion of horizons." It is obvious that Khwajeh Shams al-Din Mohammad Hafez composed his ghazals seven hundred years ago and read his story into the ear of history. You and I, who are today the audience of these poems, belong to a different context, time, and historical horizon. But this does not prevent the important matter that we strive to the best of our ability, in the light of our lived experience here and now, to become the "audience" of these poems and to understand them; an address that takes place in today's horizon and is the product of our creative and methodical encounter with the text. Of course, in this kind of dialectical encounter with the text, the beliefs, values, attitudes, and the "soul" and "world" of you and me, which have changed over time, pour forth, play an important role in the "process" of addressing the text, and create novel "products" and place them before others." Quoted from the book: "Velvety Whispers," Volume Two. Author: Soroush Dabbagh https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdrpVwpKf7D/?stkn=MmJlbnc2dGV1d284

Iranian women's continental and world sports medals are an excellent case study of the "possibility of reform" and what a progressive reformist movement can achieve through gradual, sustainable gains. Women's sports in Iran still fall far short of the capacity of Iranian women and of our aspirations and goals, but compared to three decades ago, it has seen continuous and remarkable bottom-up growth that no past government has managed to halt. The administrators and athletes who managed to make such slow and steady progress within an institutional and cultural environment full of obstacles are an instructive model for difficult reforms. The step-by-step path-clearing of countless administrators and athletes, patient gradualism, consensus-building among forces that fiercely resisted the growth and freedom of women's sports, the perseverance, and the refusal to be discouraged by the obstacles that both radical ends of the political spectrum placed in the way of women's sports—all of this is worth studying and learning from. Congratulations to us on these valuable achievements, and hats off to all the actors in this long process, especially our women athletes themselves, their coaches, and the capacity-building, path-opening administrators who, under difficult conditions, have built sustainable and irreversible achievements. @jalaeipour

[Kayhan_online] 🔰 Iran Cultural Week to Be Held in Four Russian Cities
🔸The Deputy for…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Kayhan_online

🔰 Iran Cultural Week to Be Held in Four Russian Cities

🔸The Deputy for Scientific and Cultural Cooperation at the Organization of Culture and Islamic Communication announced that the Cultural Week of the Islamic Republic of Iran will be held in four cities — Moscow, Saint Petersburg, Kazan, and Astrakhan — featuring 13 cultural, artistic, scientific, and specialized programs.

🔸Hossein Divsalar, noting the scope of the event, said: This edition of Iran Cultural Week has been designed to present a comprehensive picture of "historical Iran, cultural Iran, and contemporary Iran," and efforts have been made to introduce not only the country's civilizational and cultural heritage but also Iran's present-day capacities in art, knowledge, technology, and cultural products to Russian audiences. He described the geographical reach and diversity of the programs as hallmarks of this edition, adding: In addition to Moscow, programs will be held in Saint Petersburg, Kazan, and Astrakhan. A performance by the Iranian National Music Orchestra at the historic Bolshoi Hall in Moscow, a film and animation week, special programs for children and teenagers, scientific and academic sessions, and a large cultural and artistic exhibition are among the planned events.

🔸The Deputy of the Organization of Culture and Islamic Communication also announced a special focus on creative industries at this event, saying: Areas such as cinema and animation, toys, computer games, and fashion and apparel have been given attention in this edition, and alongside product showcases, specialized sessions and trade negotiations between Iranian and Russian professionals will be held to pave the way for joint cooperation and the entry of Iranian creative products and services into the Russian market. Divsalar, emphasizing that Iran Cultural Week should not be limited to a series of one-off programs, stated: One of the main goals of this event is to build lasting connections among artists, academics, cultural figures, and professional organizations of the two countries.

🔸To that end, the negotiations and connections established during the Cultural Week will be followed up after the programs conclude, in order to lay the groundwork for joint projects and the continuation of cultural cooperation between Iran and Russia.

🎒 Economic sanctions and the educational future of children

There was a time when economic sanctions were presented as an alternative to war, and many hoped this approach could resolve international disputes without war and destruction, while others dismissed it as ineffective. But as time passed, these assumptions were met with fundamental doubts. It gradually became clear that economic sanctions leave irreversible damage in people's lives.

Mohammad Javad Dashti-Manesh, an economic researcher, examines in this piece one of the studies conducted on the intergenerational effects of sanctions on the educational future of Iranian children, emphasizing that economic pressures must not be allowed to narrow children's educational opportunities and growth.

The findings of this study show that the long-term damage of sanctions manifests in ways such as the cancellation of remedial and supplementary classes, and even dropping out of school, and in the years to come, it will impose itself in the form of limited job and income opportunities on the generation that sits behind school desks today.

◀️ Seyyed Abbas Araghchi, the Foreign Minister of the Islamic Republic of Iran, who has traveled to New York to attend the annual session of the United Nations General Assembly, met and held talks on Wednesday morning on the sidelines of the session with Johann Wadephul, the Foreign Minister of Germany.

◀️ During this meeting, views were exchanged on bilateral relations between Iran and Germany as well as regional and international issues.

◀️ Our country's Foreign Minister, while outlining the positions of the Islamic Republic of Iran regarding international developments, stated that rebuilding trust in the functioning of the United Nations requires all governments to adhere to the principles and objectives of the Charter and international law, and criticized the conduct of European countries, including Germany, for their appeasement of America's law-breaking and bullying.

◀️ The Foreign Minister also, referring to the ongoing occupation and warmongering by the Zionist regime in the West Asia region, described Germany's military and political support, along with that of certain other European countries, as a major factor in the continuation of this regime's crimes against the countries of the region, and stressed the need to stop this kind of complicity in crimes, end impunity, and hold the occupying regime accountable.

◀️ The Foreign Minister further, while explaining Iran's responsible approach in resorting to diplomacy regarding Iran's peaceful nuclear issue, noted: No party can disregard Iran's goodwill in the negotiations and America's and the Zionist regime's military aggression against Iran in the middle of the talks, and portray Iran as the cause of insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz.

◀️ Our country's Foreign Minister emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran has conveyed logical conditions and requirements for advancing diplomacy to the American side, and stressed that restoring security to the region requires an end to America's interventionist and aggressive actions against Iran.

◀️ During this meeting, views were also exchanged on bilateral relations and diplomatic and consular consultations between the two countries.

entry.title: [jalaeipour] Israel, in violation of the UN Charter, has attacked the capitals of its…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

Israel, in violation of the UN Charter, has attacked the capitals of its neighbors, and numerous instances of violations of international humanitarian law have been documented regarding its actions, yet it maintains its nuclear arsenal without accepting similar restrictions. In contrast, Iran — which for two centuries has not waged any war except in self-defense — is targeted with sanctions and attacks, while its nuclear facilities remain under the safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Regarding the Strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said they have tried to close this strait to Iran, while they themselves have used the same route to transfer missiles and weapons to the region. The law of the sea considers such a situation illegal. The 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea — to some of whose rules Washington refers but which it has not itself ratified — stipulates that ships passing through an international strait must refrain from any threat or use of force against the coastal states of that strait. Under the rule of innocent passage as well, a ship whose passage serves an attack on a coastal state no longer qualifies as "innocent passage." Iran will not accept being deprived of its territorial waters while others use those same waters to transfer instruments of war against it.

Pezeshkian concluded by emphasizing the indivisibility of security: security either exists for all countries of the region or for no one. This idea has a long history. The logical point

Masoud Pezeshkian has presumably prepared the text of his speech for addressing the UN General Assembly, and it is unlikely that he would change it for any reason.

If I were in his place, however, I would try to occupy the "logical" position so that no justification remains for exerting pressure on the country.

The perennial issue confronting the Islamic Republic has been whether it is, in and of itself, a threat to some countries, or whether some countries are a threat to it.

If the president believes in the latter, he must state it explicitly and, for example, say: the Islamic Republic, in and of itself, is not hostile to any country in this world, and absent threats from them, all the problems that have arisen can be resolved within the framework of international laws, regulations, and norms. A clear, unambiguous, and unqualified declaration of this single point is occupying the logical position, and it will be met with a welcome from the general body of countries.

Uttering vague, general, and ambiguous sentences with the aim of satisfying all the disparate domestic forces will yield nothing but the hardship of a long journey.

🔴ExxonMobil has spent millions of dollars on the local community, yet the people living next to its carbon project are protesting
Exxon's strange social responsibility: millions spent, one unhappy community
✍️Naft Khabar:
🚨ExxonMobil has spent money on the local community, provided equipment to emergency responders, established scholarships, and its employees have put in thousands of hours of volunteer work. On paper, nearly every element of a corporate social responsibility program is there. And yet, some of the people who are supposed to live alongside one of the company's largest carbon storage projects in Texas are protesting, saying their concerns about water, safety, and the future of their community have not been heard enough.
🚨What makes the story of ExxonMobil's Rose project so intriguing is precisely this contradiction: a company that spends money on its host community, while that same community has questions and objections about its project.
🚨Over the course of 13 years, roughly 53 million tons of carbon dioxide are set to be injected deep underground in southeastern Texas. Exxon says the Rose CCS project is part of the solution for cutting emissions from America's heavy industries. But local residents have a simpler question: if the carbon from big industries is going to be buried beneath our land, who can guarantee our water, our safety, and the future of this region?
🚨The Texas Railroad Commission, the state body that regulates oil, gas, and underground storage, issued the project permit in September by a two-to-one vote. The key detail was that the dissenting vote came not from an environmental group, but from one of the commission's own three members.

entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory. Teach us to love Iran not when it aligns with our wishes, but precisely at the moment when we are angry with it, complaining about its rulers, and seeing its future as dark. God, protect us from the temptation of those saviors who must first set the land ablaze in order to build their promised tomorrow on its ashes. Do not let us be among those who sacrifice independence for the sake of freedom; the people for the sake of power; and Iran for the sake of proving their own righteousness. How easy it is to stand at a distance and prescribe courage for a people who must pay the price. How easy it is to want war when someone else's child must die in it. How easy it is to call destruction a "transition" when the house that is collapsing is not our house. God, save us from addiction to hatred; from that hatred that no longer wants truth, does not want a solution, and does not even want victory; it only wants the other to be destroyed, even if in the process, the homeland too is wounded. Give us the maturity to distinguish between opposition and revenge, between protest and destruction, between hope and illusion, and between saving a nation and seizing its future. God, do not let us one day become so thirsty for power that we shake the hand of any foreigner who promises tomorrow. Do not let us turn foreign policy from a strategy for Iran's interests into a tool for factional strife; today in the name of this group and tomorrow in the name of that group, but always at the expense of the country that must remain above us all. Do not let us put national security on the table of personal interest; for a contract, for wealth, for a position, for a share of power, or to guarantee our own future, let us not make the future of a people pay the price—a people who have no share in our bargain. Do not let us become so disgusted with today that we imagine any tomorrow as liberation, simply because it is different. Do not let us invoke the name of the people but in private think only of our own position after the storm. If we speak, let it not be for a share in tomorrow's power. If we oppose, let it not be to negotiate with potential victors. If we stand, let it not be in the ranks of this camp or that camp, but alongside a people who are always the first victims of the game of power. God, teach us that sometimes patriotism is not a shout, not a flag, not a slogan, but the ability to say a single "no": no to tyranny, no to disintegration, no to war, no to dependency, no to revenge, and no to a future that must be built by destroying Iran today.

entry.title: [jalaeipour] God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory. Teach us to love Iran not when it bends to our wishes, but precisely in the moment we are furious with it, complaining about its rulers, and seeing its future as bleak. God, protect us from the temptation of those saviors who must first set the land ablaze so they can build their promised tomorrow on its ashes. Do not let us become among those who sacrifice independence for the sake of freedom; the people for the sake of power; and Iran for the sake of proving themselves right. How easy it is to stand far away and write prescriptions of courage for a people who must pay the price. How easy it is to call for war when it is someone else's child who must die in it. How easy it is to call destruction a "transition" when the house collapsing is not our own. God, deliver us from addiction to hatred; from that hatred that no longer seeks truth, no longer seeks a solution, and does not even seek victory; it only wants the other to be destroyed, even if the homeland itself is wounded in the process. Give us the maturity to tell the difference between opposition and revenge, between protest and destruction, between hope and delusion, and between saving a nation and seizing its future. God, do not let us one day grow so thirsty for power that we clasp the hand of any foreigner who promises tomorrow. Do not let us turn foreign policy from prudence in service of Iran's interests into a weapon of factional strife; today in the name of one group and tomorrow in the name of another, but always at the expense of the country that must remain above us all. Do not let us put national security on the table of personal gain; for a contract, for wealth, for a position, for a share of power, or to secure our own future, let us not make a people pay with their future who have no stake in our bargain. Do not let us grow so sick of today that we mistake any tomorrow for liberation, simply because it is different. Do not let us invoke the name of the people on our lips while in private thinking only of our own standing after the storm. If we speak, let it not be for a share in the tomorrow of power. If we oppose, let it not be to cut a deal with would-be victors. If we stand, let it not be in the ranks of this camp or that camp, but alongside a people who are always the first victims of the game of power. God, teach us that sometimes patriotism is not a shout, not a flag, not a slogan, but the ability to say a single "no": no to tyranny, no to disintegration, no to war, no to dependency, no to revenge, and no to a future that can only be built by destroying Iran today.

A senior official of the Islamic Republic has said Tehran has proposed that if the United States reduces military pressure and takes initial steps to end the blockade of Iran's ports, it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and return to negotiations with Washington. Kyodo reported that Tehran's new proposal has been approved by "Mojtaba Khamenei," the Leader of the Islamic Republic, and the Supreme National Security Council. The Iranian official did not specify whether the proposal means Tehran is backing away from part of the seven conditions previously put forward for negotiations and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. According to Kyodo's report, the Supreme National Security Council had decided on 25 Mordad that if America does not end the blockade of Iran's ports within 45 days, the Islamic Republic would reserve the option of attacking American forces again. That deadline is now approaching. At the same time, a senior Iranian official has told "Reuters" that the Islamic Republic's delegation at the United Nations General Assembly in New York has full authority to revive diplomatic talks with America, and the details of a possible agreement can be discussed through mediating countries in New York. The Iranian official ruled out the possibility of a meeting between "Masoud Pezeshkian" and "Donald Trump" on the sidelines of the General Assembly, but said that "the possibility of moving toward an agreement" still exists. @VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

What would you plan? What would you learn? What would you start doing?🔹Now ask: Which part of that same plan can I carry out with the time I have now?If we want a longer life in order to read, to learn, to travel, or to be with our loved ones, why not bring whatever share of those things is possible into our lives today?🔹 We don't have the opportunity to do everything; the opportunity to do some things is still thereWe cannot say that if I had three hundred years to live, I would do such-and-such, but since my life is shorter, I won't even go near it.🔹If we don't have the opportunity to read a hundred books, we can read ten. If we cannot see all the lands we long for, perhaps seeing one of them is still possible. The limitedness of opportunity does not erase the value of what is still within reach.▪️ Let us not postpone life for a greater opportunity🔹We may say, I know that one day I must die, but why not fifty years from now? When those fifty years arrive, we may repeat this same request and want more time again.In the meantime, we must be careful that the wish for a longer life does not keep us from tending to this very life. We can accept the limitation of time and move our plans forward in accordance with the time and capacity we have.What is that task we have set aside for a longer life? Of that same task, how much can we begin today?📚 A lecture on the book "A Philosophical Guide for Midlife"@mostafamalekian

In sum, in recent years we have not treated our water resources properly and have created many problems in our country's environmental and territorial foundations, the most important of which can be summarized as: the drying up of the country's important lakes and wetlands such as Hor al-Azim, Shadegan, Gavkhouni, Jazmurian, Hamoun, and Lake Urmia; the severe drop in groundwater levels across the country's important plains and land subsidence; the growth of dust centers; the problem of aquatic and terrestrial life and pollution in the downstream stretches of rivers; and seawater intrusion into rivers. Therefore, now that there is a possibility of a large volume of water falling from the sky, we can welcome it with two approaches. One approach, rooted in fear and threat, is to focus all our efforts on safely channeling the huge volume of water to the sea, which may also alleviate a few of the above-mentioned problems along its path. But the other approach focuses on making the utmost beneficial use of this yield so that we can solve many of the above-mentioned problems beforehand. Pursuing the second approach, which is certainly in the interest of our country's present and future, requires precise planning, structural works, and, more broadly, a change in how we view this phenomenon. Planning for flood spreading, maximum recharge of aquifers in the country's critical plains, the planned channeling of floods toward wetlands, channeling floods toward dust centers, and finally the safe channeling of floods toward downstream areas and the sea — all of this can be seen as the result of shifting our view of El Niño from a curse to a blessing, and can turn our fear of facing it into an opportunity. And in the end, we can ask ourselves: if the predictions come true, will we be good hosts to welcome El Niño's water yield?

entry.title:
[mohsenhesammazaheri] 🔸The Loss of a Mediator🔸
If we were to describe any figure with a single…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mohsenhesammazaheri

🔸The Loss of a Mediator🔸

If we were to describe any figure with a single word, the word that fits Ayatollah Seyyed Mousa Shubeyri Zanjani (who passed away last night) is "mediator."

Despite being considered, in terms of his jurisprudential orientation, among the traditionalist jurists of the seminary, and despite not being devoid of taste or conviction in politics and history—as is evident from his scattered remarks and writings (including in the highly readable book collection "A Sip from the Sea")—he had his own distinct and particular social and political demeanor. In the past two or three decades, he played a role that others were incapable of fulfilling: the role of "mediator" between the system and the religious currents and individuals it had cast out. Shubeyri Zanjani was a "dragoman" for translating the words of two groups who did not understand each other's language. That is why knots that could not be untied through law and conventional political methods were sometimes loosened by a single phone call from him, and challenges that could have spiraled into crises were sometimes defused by a single piece of advice from him. These mediations were, of course, typically behind the scenes and never publicized—and that, too, was part of his way of being.

Because of this role he played, Shubeyri was beloved by all sides. He both associated with the martyred Leader and would recite the funeral prayer for clerics critical of the system, and the door of his home remained open every day to all political and religious currents. Undoubtedly, his humble and tolerant character also contributed to this.

In religious matters as well, although he is classified among the traditional jurists, he took a different approach there too. Unlike them, he did not use his position, standing, and influence to pursue religious identity-driven concerns, and did not seek to pile up a calendar of Shia occasions and to fatten rituals. On the contrary, he was critical of the excessive expansion of rituals.

That said, if the loss of Mr. Shubeyri Zanjani is considered a scholarly loss for the seminaries, it will be a functional and institutional blow for the system and for Iranian society as well—one that could disrupt the relations between the system and certain seminary and religious currents. Although Shubeyri was not considered among the first-tier maraji' in terms of the organizational structure of the marja'iyya, and did not have extensive organizations and numerous offices, and the number of his followers did not extend beyond the circle of certain seminary elites and his fellow townspeople, his loss creates a void in the institution of Shia marja'iyya in Iran that cannot be filled—especially in the current critical conditions, when Iranian society, more than ever, needs those who play the role of mediator in various arenas.

✍️ Mohsen Hesam Mazaheri
Republished in the Iran newspaper (1405/06/31)
1405/06/30 @mohsenhesammazaheri

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] A benevolent and cautious authority. I have heard valuable insights from…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

A benevolent and cautious authority. I have heard valuable insights from Gholamhossein Karbaschi about the political and jurisprudential approach and personal character of Ayatollah Seyyed Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani. In the late 1340s and early 1350s, Mr. Karbaschi was one of the distinguished students of the late Mr. Shobeiri. According to what I have heard, Ayatollah Shobeiri was cautious in both jurisprudence and politics — the very principle that traditional Shia scholars regarded as a sign of piety. Caution means examining a matter from all sides before expressing an opinion or taking action — in other words, never wading into water without first finding a crossing — which is precisely what some clerics claiming revolutionary fervor have completely abandoned and cast aside! A cautious authority is extremely watchful of his tongue and his actions, is not one for controversy, does not level accusations against others, and for this reason is usually silent or very taciturn. The late Mr. Shobeiri, in addition to this, was inclined toward tolerance and benevolence in political matters. Although he did not speak of it, in practice he would act to the best of his ability to redress injustice or to free from political entanglement those he knew closely. In 1397, the presence of the late Ayatollah Shobeiri at the home of Sheikh Abdullah Nouri, along with the presence of Seyyed Mohammad Khatami, provoked the anger of Sheikh Mohammad Yazdi in his capacity as "Secretary of the Supreme Council of the Seminary"! Mr. Yazdi, who despite a decade of heading the Judiciary had gained no share of self-restraint, publicly reproached an authority who, in terms of jurisprudential stature, was far above him, asking why he had gone to visit people like Khatami and Nouri without his permission! Mr. Yazdi imagined that certain official positions had placed him in a position of lordship such that he could command and forbid an authority of the caliber of Mr. Shobeiri! Ayatollah Shobeiri, in accordance with his conduct, showed no reaction to Mr. Yazdi's behavior and remained silent — a silence that was full of things said and unsaid. At the same time, Hassan Rahimpour Azghadi also accused traditional seminarians of promoting secularism and deemed them secular themselves. Mr. Azghadi's reference was apparently to people like the late Mr. Shobeiri, who did not act and did not speak according to his "revolutionary preferences"! Although Mr. Makarem and Mr. Nouri Hamedani gave a decisive response to Rahimpour Azghadi, Ayatollah Shobeiri again remained silent. In any case, may God have mercy on him and forgive him. He prayed over the bodies of scholars such as Ayatollah Montazeri and Ayatollah Sanei. Who will pray over his own body? #Ahmad_Zeidabadi @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [jalaeipour] ⚫️ Given my interest in the sociology of religious authority and the years…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

⚫️ Given my interest in the sociology of religious authority and the years of research I've done in this area, friends repeatedly put this question to me: which marja' taqlid in Qom do you personally prefer most? Each time, my answer was Ayatollah al-Uzma Shobeiry Zanjani. A first-rate jurist, and outstanding in rijal. But he combined this jurisprudential and scholarly standing with qualities that are rarer still. He, his household, and those around him lived with great integrity and an intense sensitivity to financial propriety. He was humble in a way seldom seen and indifferent to the conventional protocols of marja'iyat, and despite absolute jurisprudential authority, he made no effort whatsoever to attract devotees and followers or to acquire prestige, status, fame, or power. He was spiritual—a "man of God"—and his serenity, his piety, and his prayers were a sight to behold. He was one of those of whom it is said, in a saying attributed to Jesus Christ: "Whoever's sight reminds you of God, whose knowledge adds to your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire goodness." In addition to his morning teaching, he held a gathering at his home an hour before maghrib, which in my view—if the hawza's "scholarly gathering" were ever to be registered as an "intangible heritage"—would be a perfect example; and for me, a mere outsider, every time I attended, its atmosphere and details were a spectacle to behold. He also possessed a cultivated aesthetic sensibility, evident in, among other things, his beautiful handwriting and his exceedingly delicate gaze and body language. He never sought perks, resources, or privileges, and he used his considerable spiritual influence over the system's high-ranking officials solely to unblock people's difficulties and help the oppressed. A lovable spiritual jurist. May his soul rest in peace.https://t.me/ShobeiryZanjani/6357@jalaeipour

Velayati said it, and Yousef Pezeshkian took the heat for it! The baseless uproar that extremist media have whipped up against Yousef Pezeshkian, the president's son, pardon the expression, is like an unspeakable proverb! In a remark, Yousef Pezeshkian challenged some hardline forces who want the war to continue, asking them: if they're so fond of war, why do they protest against its dire economic consequences? War, after all, brings every kind of economic pressure in its wake. So Yousef Pezeshkian said that if some people hold up Yemen's Houthis as the proper model for fighting, why don't they accept their model of consumption too, instead of pressuring the government with every wave of inflation and rising prices? Yousef Pezeshkian's sentence is "conditional" — built on an if and a then. The hardliners, however, have stripped out the condition and made it seem as though the president's son repeated Ali Akbar Velayati's famous line. Mr. Velayati, 8 years ago around these very days, had said: "Let's learn from the Yemenis how they resist threats and sanctions. Instead of clothes, they wear a loincloth and carry weapons in their hands, with a few pieces of dry bread in their hands, on foot — and the Saudis were left helpless against them." Mr. Velayati's remarks that day drew sharp criticism from political forces, but the circles that rushed to defend his words back then have today, by attributing the exact opposite of that statement to Yousef Pezeshkian, attacked and reviled him! Truly, Luqman the Wise must have learned fairness, honesty, and sincerity from such a crowd! Apparently, under such conditions, being Pezeshkian's son is no blessing — quite the opposite — but rather an easy target for any kind of foul language and an extremely short wall to climb over! God forbid!

entry.title:
[bamotamem] The B&R Program – Part Three
My take is that you can learn as much about…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

The B&R Program – Part Three

My take is that you can learn as much about China's ideas, strategies, and orientations from B&R as you can from BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.

I know that comparing a program to an organization, a forum, or a treaty is flawed. But I'm making this point in the sense that within B&R, China's hands are free and it isn't bogged down in coordinating with multiple governments. At the same time, it has to allocate resources directly to projects. So maybe in BRICS and the SCO, there are moments of pleasantries and what you might call political flirting, but in B&R there's no room for those games. They have to genuinely lay out their decisions and policies clearly and transparently, and actually implement them.

Although it has never been officially stated outright, in my view (a personal interpretation), one of the main reasons China at one point encouraged Iran and Saudi Arabia to negotiate and clear up their grievances probably comes back to B&R. Setting aside the things that get written on paper, signed, and photographed (Iranian officials have racked up plenty of those photos with China), in practice China's largest volume of B&R cooperation in our region has been with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Iraq. Cooperation with Iran hasn't been insignificant either. But sanctions, banking restrictions, and other considerations have made the scale of cooperation different.

The horizon China has for B&R spans several decades. And naturally, it aligns the decisions, policies, and resources it allocates with this project as much as possible.

In a way, you could call it a super-framework for economic and investment affairs.

By the way, Pakistan is also one of China's close partners in this program. Of course, beyond all that, Pakistan has a very deep relationship with China. In the media, it's usually referred to as an ironclad relationship (China doesn't throw around such terms and expressions lightly).

The last point worth paying attention to is that China insists strongly on defining its interactions — whether in B&R or in other cooperations — as a partnership, and emphasizes that it is not the type for alliance. The logic is that a partnership makes sense between two parties. But an alliance is usually formed against a third country, or assumes (or creates) a third rival.

This strategy leads China, in many instances, not to behave the way its partners expect it to.

entry.title: [jalaeipour] The book "In Defense of Universal Basic Services" rests on three theoretical…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

The book "In Defense of Universal Basic Services" rests on three theoretical pillars: human needs, the capability approach, and foundational economics and provisioning systems. The authors argue that compared to Universal Basic Income (UBI), the idea of Universal Basic Services (UBS)—by rebuilding social infrastructure and collective consumption while also enhancing efficiency and ecological sustainability—strengthens equality and solidarity as well, and is politically feasible because it is incremental and adaptable in nature. The authors see this idea as a path toward reclaiming the collective ideal that has been weakened under neoliberal pressures. They regard health, education, housing, transportation, care for children and the elderly, and access to digital information as necessities whose provision must be guaranteed for all through user participation and co-production in identifying needs and designing services, and through a combination of organizations—with Universal Basic Income serving merely as a supplement to cover non-service costs and to increase households' bargaining power, because if the provisioning pillar of Universal Basic Services is weak, basic income leads to the commodification and minimization of basic services.

entry.summary:

Source: @bamotamem

The B&R Program – Part Two
The Chinese government launched the Belt & Road Initiative in 2013. "Belt" refers to the land route. "Road" here doesn't mean a road; it means a route — a maritime route.
The idea behind B&R is China's development of land and sea routes to the West (specifically Europe), and roughly 150 countries are involved. That is, China went and talked to countries one by one and worked out a framework with each of them regarding what kinds of cooperation it could have with them along this route.
There are two books about this, written by two Jonathans!
The first Jonathan is Jonathan Hillman, who wrote the book The Emperor's New Road (China and the Project of the Century).
The second Jonathan, Jonathan Fulton, has written a book on the ins and outs of the B&R program in the Arab world, which hasn't been published yet. But his previous writings and the book he previously wrote titled The Relationship Between China and the Persian Gulf Monarchies (which he also worked on with Routledge) show that he examines these kinds of topics very precisely and thoroughly.
If you don't have the patience to read the works of these two or similar material, talk to one of these AI services, or when you ask a question, tell it to also pay attention to B&R or what these people say in the context — that works too.

entry.title: [bamotamem] The Chinese government and today's Middle East situation – The B&R Program…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

The Chinese government and today's Middle East situation – The B&R Program – Part One

It seems to me that friends who these days are looking to analyze the current situation in the Middle East and examine possible future scenarios are paying particularly close attention to Iran, America, and the role of regional players, while giving China a smaller share of attention.

Yet China's decisions in recent years have played an important role in the region – both in places where it intervened contrary to expectations, such as Iran-Saudi relations, and in places where, despite expectations, it did not intervene or intervened only very minimally.

And now that Iran's connections with the world have become more limited, a large portion of the fears and hopes of the country's policymakers and decision-makers naturally circles back to China.

The first thing that usually comes to mind is that China is almost the only buyer of Iran's oil, and from another angle, Iran is a cheap energy supplier and a source of access to mines and underground resources for China.

I feel that this view is not enough to understand China's decisions and policies, the actions it has taken in the region in recent years, the decisions it is making now, and its positions on events that will unfold in the region in the future.

My suggestion to friends who are interested in this topic is to read up a bit on China's Belt & Road program. Aside from being a fascinating subject, it opens our minds to China's way of looking at many regional and international issues.

Tonight, in a separate post, I'll write a few more sentences about this.

(Of course, I don't have any particular expertise in this subject. I've read a few books and articles out of personal curiosity. Dig around yourselves – you'll find more information.)

Today, the energy imbalance is no longer just a temporary constraint on the petrochemical industry; it is an issue directly tied to the competitiveness, profitability, and future development of this industry.

Yashar and Farnaz, in pursuit of scapegoating Iran
🔹In the middle of his exposé clip about the trusts, Yashar Soltani — without mentioning America's prior violations — names the Stability political faction as the cause of the understanding's collapse.
🔹This is the same narrative previously put forward in Farnaz Fassihi's report in the New York Times; a narrative claiming that the action of a rogue group in Iran destroyed the diplomatic opportunity that existed in the understanding between Iran and America.
But what is the hidden reality?
🔹The most important clause of the understanding was the acceptance of Iranian arrangements in the administration of the strait. That is, in exchange for accepting certain obligations, Iran had secured its right to manage and maintain its own particular arrangements in the world's most important oil passage.
🔹From day one, America was determined to violate this clause and, as with the violation of other clauses, to normalize it. The failure to release the assets and the failure to establish a ceasefire on other fronts are clear examples of these violations.
🔹Logically, Iran, in defense of its gains under the understanding, should have shown itself to be serious and, during the transitional period, should have stood firm on its rights so that it could secure its right in the final agreement.
🔹The opening of the southern corridor in the strait was a fundamental violation of the understanding by America — an action that, if left unanswered, would have practically rendered the main clause of the understanding ineffective.
🔹After several days of warnings, the timely action of striking the vessels and not remaining indifferent to the violation of Iran's rights under the understanding was defensible on the part of the country's decision-makers.
🔹The inverted narrative of the story that portrays Iran as responsible for disrupting the understanding is fabricated by Israeli and monarchist accounts and American media.
Why is this narrative important?
🔸If this reading is correct, what happened in the Strait of Hormuz was a reaction to America's clear violation of the understanding.
🔸In this framework, the one who first broke the understanding was Washington, not Iran. But the rival narrative, by swapping the roles of victim and culprit, wants to shift the political cost of this decision onto an internal faction.
🔸The narrative that "the rogues broke the understanding" is on the surface simple and attractive, but when placed alongside America's chain of violations, it collapses.
🖼The important question, however, is why should one expect Iran to remain a spectator in the face of the violation of the main clause of the understanding? And why now, instead of condemning the primary violator, is the finger of accusation pointed inward?

📢 The inevitable shift in Iranian tastes; red meat consumption drops to one-third

◀️ The Donya-e-Eqtesad newspaper has reported a significant change in the meat consumption patterns of Iranian households. According to the report, per capita red meat consumption has fallen from about 14 kilograms in the mid-1380s to roughly 5 kilograms in recent years.

◀️ At the same time, households have increasingly turned to chicken to make up for reduced access to red meat, with chicken's share of total meat consumption rising from about 30 percent in the 1360s to around 60 percent. That figure is said to be less than 30 percent globally.

◀️ Total per capita meat consumption has also dropped from about 35 kilograms in 1383 to 25 kilograms in 1403 — a decline of roughly 30 percent.

◀️ Donya-e-Eqtesad stressed that this trend cannot be attributed solely to a "change in taste"; the decline in households' real income and the surge in food prices have also played a major role. According to the report, meat prices rose about 5.8 times between 1400 and 1404.

◀️ Persian Gulf countries had relied on this presence by signing defense treaties, but the recent 7-month conflict destroyed these assumptions; the bases became vulnerabilities, and the IRGC, by targeting them, has depleted America's expensive and scarce air defense missiles.
◀️ Now the debate is whether rebuilding America's presence at its previous scale is financially and strategically worthwhile.

AI Mistake Brought America to the Brink of War with China

🔹 This spring, an AI analysis sounded the alarm for the Americans. Based on incorrect information, they believed that a Chinese ship was transporting components of a nuclear weapons program.

🔹 According to a CNN report citing informed sources, the US military prepared to seize the ship; armed US military personnel were getting ready to board the vessel, and military aircraft were also standing by in the sky.

🔹 However, only shortly before the start of this planned operation, it became clear that the AI had misidentified the ship's cargo. No further details about the contents of the ship were mentioned, but sources told CNN that the AI report was "completely incorrect." 🔸The key point is that this sacrificing class generally comes from the weaker strata of society: owners of small homes, few or no cars, minimal consumption of water, electricity, and gasoline — those whose entire share of the revolution's table is a meager subsidy of at most 400,000 tomans. These people have been on the streets since the beginning of the war, have endured a hard livelihood, and unlike some managers and officials, have raised no complaints.

Why is nothing said about the country's main assets being squandered in banks and state-owned companies, or about astronomical salaries and billion-toman bonuses?

🔸The main problem is not the low costs of the "self-sacrificing" people, but the management model and unnecessary extravagance, luxury per-diem allowances and billion-toman trips, lack of planning, and inefficiency. If these squanderings are stopped, there is no need to ask the people who carry the burden of the economy on their own shoulders to live like Yemenis! The sent-forth nation of Iran is the model for the nations and free people of the world. This volume of entitlement toward the nation has no name but mismanagement and shamelessness.

Footnote: I should also add that my observations pertain to a period after the end of the main war and should not be generalized to the past. Based on what I know from the days of the war, and in particular from the gatherings following the martyrdom of Ali Larijani, at that stage these gatherings were far more widespread and, in terms of class composition, generation, and social types, far more diverse as well. By the time I arrived in Tehran and began my field observations, the situation had changed considerably: the core of the gatherings appeared more homogeneous in terms of class, style of dress, religious rituals, and social type. Therefore, the description I offer in this section pertains to that specific period of observation, not to the social composition of the gatherings throughout the entire war. Put differently, the very shift in the composition of the crowd may itself be part of the evolution of this phenomenon in the interval between the days of the war and the period that followed. Nevertheless, distinguishing those three strata in the nighttime gatherings of the months after the forty-day war seems important.

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

But you could see that the sustained presence of part of society in the public space was effectively producing a different image of the street: the street was not entirely in the hands of a single force. And it is precisely at this point that internal simplification can also ruin the analysis. If, because of the radical slogans of the third group, we treat the entire gathering as a factional movement, we have conflated the first body with the third group. If, because of the presence of needy people next to the mokebs, we assume the whole crowd was "brought in with food," we have substituted a social situation for a political explanation. And in the opposite direction, if, because of the presence of families and their genuine emotions, we deny any formal organizing or factional activity on the margins of the gatherings, we have once again erased part of the scene. Perhaps the most important difference between a television report and field observation is this. The camera passes over the crowd and turns a thousand people into one "people." The politician speaks from behind a desk about those same thousand people and turns them into one "current." Social media clips a few seconds of the most radical slogan and turns a thousand people into those same few who shouted loudest. But when you walk among them yourself, this unity quickly comes apart. One has come to recite prayers. One has come to say that in wartime you don't stay home. One has come because it's night and the square is crowded. One stands next to the mokeb because life has become expensive. And one is waiting for the ceremony to end so he can just begin his own political work. They are all in one street; but they are not necessarily in one gathering.3

Trump's threats today must be seen against the backdrop of the dead end in which America has become mired because of the war. In this context, the problem for Trump is less about entering a new phase of the war than about finding a way out of it — an exit that is apparently meant to be constructed in two stages. First, using threats and pressure to force Iran into a new round of negotiations; then, if that path fails, carrying out a major operation aimed at upending the existing equations and creating a turning point to end the war. In other words, Trump wants to use escalating pressure not to prolong the war, but to create the conditions for leaving it. But this roadmap, much like Lyndon Johnson's strategy for ending the Vietnam War, overlooks one fundamental variable: the self-escalating nature of war itself, and the fact that military pressure does not necessarily produce the desired political outcome. Indeed, the very threat meant to steer negotiations toward a result becomes a factor that deepens and intensifies the war even further. Consequently, if Trump is genuinely seeking to exit the war, he should take his cue less from Democrat Johnson and more from Republican Nixon — a Nixon whose negotiations with North Vietnam rested on two points: first, an acceptance of the limits of American power, and second, recognition of the other side.@katechon6

entry.title:
[ahmadzeidabad] Unipolar and multipolar!
Has the world order ever been unipolar? Some call the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

Unipolar and multipolar!

Has the world order ever been unipolar? Some call the order of the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union unipolar, but the reality is otherwise. In my view, the world has never seen a unipolar order and never will!

Is the world now heading toward a multipolar order? In my view, a "multipolar order" is the most dangerous possible state for the world, because it is not order at all — it is the very essence of disorder and instability! The emergence of a hypothetical multipolar situation in the world would mean the end of our world through devastating wars waged with weapons of mass destruction! When we speak of a "pole," the conflict of interests is its most important defining feature. The conflict of interests ultimately leads to war, leaving destruction and annihilation in its wake. If, to avoid war, a mechanism for resolving disputes were defined, then in its light the very concept of a pole would fade — because a dispute-resolution mechanism is nothing other than the definition and pursuit of common interests, and once common interests come into play, the pole loses its conventional meaning.

Today we are faced with a world in which every member plays a role proportionate to its own capacity. No member is uncontested, and no member is without influence.

A combination of the types and degrees of influence of approximately 200 members of the international community shapes the order of today's world. An infinitely intricate network, grounded in deep mutual interdependence among the members of the global community, has taken shape — one that renders obsolete all the traditional concepts customary in the international system.

We Iranians, whatever our political and ideological leanings, seem in our subconscious to be influenced by bipolar thinking — or rather by the dualistic worldview of our ancestors — and for this very reason we not only welcome polarization but are incapable of observing and understanding the world and its affairs except through its lens!

This outlook has darkened our view of reality and has cost us dearly.

As Rumi said:

Before your eyes you held a blue glass;
for that reason the world appeared blue to you.

I will explain more on this matter.

#احمد_زیدآبادی
@ahmadzeidabad
